utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes and Mr. Bourgon. Good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to continue with Mr. Josse's cross-examination. And then we see whether there is a re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This morning, General, I'm going to begin with some questions of a general nature, and I would like to ask you a little bit about the relationship between some of the top military figures in UNPROFOR. First of all, how much exposure and/or dealings did you have with General Janvier in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Chief of Staff, I did not ordinarily deal directly with General Janvier. General Smith, my commander, was responsible for those dealings, but obviously, I met him on various occasions and spoke with him. But as far as doing any business with him was concerned, in 99 per cent of the cases, General Smith was responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you spoke to Janvier what language did you use?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did he require an interpreter to understand you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he could understand me or not, but he always spoke via an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was the same true of General Gobillard, namely he always spoke to you through an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. My impression was that General Gobillard was even more dependent on interpreter than General Janvier was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you presumably had more to do with Gobillard than you did with Janvier, bearing in mind that Gobillard was posted actually in Sarajevo, albeit in a different building to you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. The second factor was that if General Smith was absent, he was ordinarily replaced by General Gobillard and then that was of course his Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I didn't understand the end of the answer. You've just said, "He was ordinarily replaced by General Gobillard and then that was of course his Chief of Staff." Explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I said was if General Smith was replaced by General Gobillard, then obviously I acted as his Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's a very minor translation issue and that's why I wanted to clarify it. Well, talking of translation issues, did you have a Dutch-English interpreter at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your English was of a high enough standard to communicate at all material times with UNPROFOR personnel using English rather than Dutch; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I never heard any complaints. I admit, though, that the first two or three weeks I had a bit of difficulty getting used to it, but after that, no more problems occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the question I'm about to ask, I want to emphasise is not a criticism at all but is a genuine inquiry. You have chosen to give evidence before this Tribunal using your own native tongue rather than English. Explain why, please.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. First, I believe that court hearings are extremely important and I do not want to run the risk that due to any possible misuse of terminology, misunderstandings might arise. Second, it's much easier for me to express myself in my native language than in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Gobillard speak English at all?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you attended meetings which involved Gobillard and Smith, how did they communicate?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Gobillard's MA acted as interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately not off the top of my head. Perhaps I could find that somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm afraid this is a bit of a trick question because I am here testing your memory because in fact this Tribunal, this Chamber, heard from this gentleman Monday and Tuesday of this week. I'll tell you his name in a moment but before I do that, perhaps you could tell us whether you recall which country he came from?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Canadian. I believe he was Canadian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Yes. And his name was Lieutenant -- I think he was a major at the time, his name was Major Fortin, for your information. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now I remember. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have the equivalent to a military assistant?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Lieutenant-Colonel Andrew De Ruiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall any UNPROFOR general in the time you were in Bosnia giving a gift or memento to any of the generals of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why was that? Was that because it wasn't the done thing or because none of them deserved it? Can you help at all?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't simply make up a reason why somebody would give a gift to a general of one of the warring parties. I don't think it's explicitly prohibited, but I think you should be very, very cautious to avoid giving the impression that you are biased in favour of one of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I take it you certainly wouldn't want to give a gift or a memento to someone you felt had behaved in a reprehensible manner?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next topic I'd like to ask you about, please, is interpreters. You mentioned yesterday that you had an interpreter called Svetlana and you told us that you did not recall her surname. Are you able to help us as to her ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And she was on the UN payroll; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: She was interpreting for you during your two conversations with Gvero, correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And she was by your side during both of those conversations?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea as to whether General Gvero had any sort of interpretive support?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't require one because all he needed to do was communicate with Svetlana and that was in his native language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at P2751? We have it up now in English. And this is a conversation that you gave evidence about yesterday relating to your talking to General Tolomir on the 9th of July at 1750. From recollection, you're saying that Svetlana was an interpreter during this conversation as well?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, let's read to yourself, by all means, the first paragraph of this conversation, where you begin by expressing your deep concern about the developing situation in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the words in the middle of that paragraph that I'm going to read out that I would draw your attention to are the following: "This was considered to be an attack on the safe area which would force UNPROFOR to defend the safe area with all means they had." That's obviously what you were telling Tolimir, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was that a threat?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the third paragraph of this conversation, you say, in the middle of that paragraph, "Moreover, since the BiH troops have been prevented to take their heavy weapons from the WCP, UNPROFOR was now forced to defend this safe area." I appreciate it was a long time ago, but tell us, as best you can, what that assertion on your part was based on?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heavy weapons of the BiH troops in the enclave were -- had been taken from them to the extent possible and stored at the weapon collection point. This means that where the troops in the enclave were shot at by heavy weapons of the VRS, they were not able to fight back in the same manner. That meant that everybody staying in the enclave received protection from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you know that the BiH troops had been prevented from taking their heavy weapons from the weapon collection points?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the weapon collection point was in Srebrenica at the compounds of one of the DutchBat companies. So without permission from DutchBat, heavy weapons could not be removed from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And this is really what I'm driving at: Had you received any information -- and I'm deliberately asking you about your recollection now -- had you received any information specifically on that point for you to make that assertion to Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no special cause for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you at that time physically know where the weapon collection point in Srebrenica was located?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I repeat that was in the town of Srebrenica, at the DutchBat Bravo Company compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you give any specific order or instruction, don't want to be too militaristic about it, to Karremans or one of his subordinates as to what they should do with these heavy weapons at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet on 9 July. On 10 July, we decided that if the BiH desired, the heavy weapons would be made available from the collection point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what happened in that regard, please?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No use was made of that opportunity, as you probably know. Otherwise, I can tell you that during the night of 10 to 11 July, the Muslim soldiers started their exfiltration to leave the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: P2973, please. This is the next conversation between you and General Tolimir on the 9th of July at 1930 hours. And on that first page, we see in the middle of the page, a long paragraph and we'll need to scroll up a bit, please. Thank you. And perhaps you could read that to yourself.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will do that. Yes. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in that paragraph, you are threatening Tolimir on at least three occasions?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't exactly count the number of times but I did threaten him that there could be a heavy reaction from the side of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The word here that we see in the middle of the paragraph is "disproportional." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. And I can explain that. That word was used deliberately, where the VRS were using artillery and mortars, and BiH didn't have the -- or the UNPROFOR didn't have the same kind of weapons, and the only possible reply to that was the use of air support, so in that sense, we would normally consider that disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what you've just said, and bearing in mind what we read in that paragraph, did you regard yourself as involved in a game of brinkmanship with General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the word power-play or brinkmanship is the right thing to say here. My only intention was to put an end to this extremely precarious situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It involved careful and considered negotiation on your part, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, if you see what contacts there had been starting from Saturday, 8 July, until the fall of the enclave on the 11th of July, from the side of the UN, and particularly from myself, several attempts were made to move the VRS to withdraw their troops and to leave the enclave before in actual fact our air attacks were started. I think that from all the documentation which is available to the Court, this is amply clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At that point in time, your job required careful, well-considered and indeed clever negotiating skills, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Had you had any training, either from your own government or army or from the United Nations, in the job that you were at that point in time being asked to perform?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to my posting, I received a training in negotiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In this country, the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A course run by the Netherlands rather than by the United Nations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a training course delivered at the Clingendael Institute here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You'd agree, wouldn't you, that this was a difficult negotiation where you, along with the other participants, were under a lot of pressure and were very much in the world spotlight? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never really experienced that sort of pressure. I think it was difficult for the outside world to follow how these negotiations went, so in this respect, I fully had to rely on myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, of course the outside world didn't know that were you speaking to Tolimir at such and such a time or Gvero, Mladic or anyone else, but there was a great deal of pressure on you, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in my experience. The only real pressure there was, how can we get out of this conflict without having to resort to the highest level of violence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you really telling the Trial Chamber that you were not under pressure, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind -- let me start again. Would you accept that the negotiations were delicate?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally. Especially for the people in the enclave, there was a lot at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you think that you were labouring under some sort of handicap, bearing in mind you were unable to use your native tongue and you were forced to use English in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time, I had been at my post at -- for about six months. No, that didn't -- that was no impediment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And of course that's why I asked you a few minutes ago why you've chosen to give your evidence in Dutch in this courtroom. It's an interesting contrast, don't you think?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. During my work there for months on end I would speak English from the morning until evening, and that is not what I'm doing now, so I'm not excluding that I couldn't do this, but it's a lot simpler to communicate in one's own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we scroll down to the bottom of this first page, we see it says there, it's Tolimir speaking, and he says, "It is the BiH offensive actions taken from the DMZ that constituted the violation of all signed agreements." Did you accept that proposition of General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot deny that from time to time BiH soldiers from the enclave would take actions outside the borders of the enclave. DutchBat personnel knew this but they were unable to stop this, point 1, because the number of troops was too limited, and because of their lack of fuel they couldn't perform any motorised patrols, so they were not in a sufficiently strong position to counter this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's a subject I'm going to return to a little later so I'm not going to spend too long on it now, but I would suggest you haven't answered my question. My question was really quite simple: Did you accept what Tolimir had said in that last sentence of page 1 of P2973?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think that the reason for the attacks in the enclave was the fact that every now and then actions were undertaken. One could take different kinds of measures against that. Surely at that specific point in time, there was no increase in BiH activities as compared to other points in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I say, I'll ask you something about that a little later, if I may. I'd like to ask you a few questions about some of your evidence of yesterday, and at page 32 of yesterday's proceedings, you talked about the entire enclave being surrounded by VRS positions and you described various artillery positions and launching systems for multiple rocket launchers. At that time, were you aware whether the VRS were actually using multiple rocket launchers in this campaign?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not able to answer that last question. I do not know whether these multiple rocket systems at that point in time had already been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then why did you mention it yesterday in response to questions from Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Colonel Karremans had reported that these weapons systems were posted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you'd had a report from Colonel Karremans that, as you say, they were situated there but you had no reports as to the -- whether or not they were used? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you've understood that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Move on to another document that you reviewed yesterday. That's P2975, please. Now, this is a two-page document. The first is the cover sheet showing that it's from the office of the commander HQ UNPROFOR, and the second is the warning to the Bosnian Serbs, attacks against the Srebrenica safe area. And we'll look at the second page, the text of this document, in a moment. But we see on the first page that it says "Message, attached is the final version of the warning to Bosnian Serbs. We have sent it as a CapSat to General Mladic and we will issue it as a press statement." Why was the office of the commander of UNPROFOR issuing this warning to Mladic as a press statement?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume that they wanted to note to the outside world how serious the situation was and that they also wanted to let the international community know that the UN were at the point perhaps of starting to use air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The United Nations were part of the propaganda war that the warring parties were engaged in, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to express myself that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, is that -- I think it may be a translation issue here. Are you not agreeing with what I'm saying or are you saying you'd rather not answer my question?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no difficulty answering your questions. And I am aware that the parties were constantly trying to involve the UN in their own propaganda. But the UN, from its side, has always done its utmost to counter that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Come on, now, General. This press release is aimed at trying to win over public opinion in favour of the United Nations. That is propaganda, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN has absolutely no need to make a favourable impression on the international community. The UN, however, does have a duty to properly inform the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the international community needed to be informed, did they, that UNPROFOR was now saying it's going to stand up to these bully boys in the VRS and we are actually going to drop some bombs on them? That's information rather than propaganda? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that you are trying to provoke me, but I think it is a duty to inform the international community that there is a very serious situation at hand which may lead to the UN being forced to deploy its heaviest means in order to solve problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Turning to the second page of the document, and the warning itself, the first sentence was read out yesterday. Perhaps you and the Trial Chamber could read it to yourselves. And having read it out, Mr. Thayer, at page 35, asked you, "Do you recall receiving information during this period of time that civilians had been killed by the VRS shelling or firing?" And your answer was, "Yes, that's correct. That was reported on repeated occasions." 12 years later, can you tell us who those reports came from?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you know how many civilians they said were killed by this type of direct targeting of UN facilities?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to correct this question to the extent that it wasn't -- it happened not only during firing at UN facilities but also during random shootings at the enclave. I can't tell you the exact number of casualties. You would need to refer to the UN reports for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were also asked a couple of pages later, at page 37, about Colonel Karremans' fear in the event that close air support was used by UNPROFOR, and you used the words that he feared, "This would lead to massive retaliation." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's how I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you said that you understood his point.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you think -- let me ask you this: That retaliation was going to be aimed, in Karremans' mind, what, at his troops or at the civilians or at both? Didn't he know? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, I think at his troops but I wouldn't exclude retaliation to the civilian population either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you think that this fear on his part was acceptable in the case of a colonel in your army?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Where a commander is also responsible for his troops, he has a duty to note the potential consequences of certain acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we saw yesterday, and if need be we could bring it up in e-court but I think probably not at the moment, that in his letter, P2974 at paragraph 10, he used the words "using CAS in all possible ways is in my opinion not feasible yet." And that letter was dated the 9th of July. You'll remember that as well, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, could we have in e-court, please, 6D153, which is your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of November of 1996. And at page 9, very bottom of the page, in this paragraph you describe events around the 6th of July, heavy fighting, describe heavy artillery, say the shelling was mostly directed at military targets and not directly against the civilian population at that point at least. And then you go on and say that the DutchBat observation posts in the south of the enclave felt threatened by the presence of VRS troops so close to their OPs. "Colonel Karremans wanted air presence to show the VRS that he had the capability to use these aircraft. I did not give permission for the use of air presence. I explained to him that if you use the presence of your aircraft too often without really attacking, it loses its effectiveness. This conversation was made by telephone." Now, General, I appreciate that there is a difference between air presence and actually dropping bombs from an airplane, but beyond that, this seems quite a volte face between the 7th of July -- the 6th of July, I beg your pardon, and the 9th of July on the part of Karremans, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation had changed. On 6 July, there was a single observation post that was being threatened. In the post-air-strike guidance issued at the end of May, it is indicated explicitly that if troops are threatened that are still in a position to withdraw that that is preferable to using air weapons. On 9 July, the situation had changed considerably. It was no longer about threatening a single observation post. In this case, the entire enclave was attacked and the civilian population in the enclave was threatened in this case. The situation that had materialised made use of air weapons opportune beyond any doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So in reality, you are saying that in Karremans' mind, there was a big difference between air presence and air support?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what this is about. What matters is that while we didn't consider use of air weapons opportune on 6 July, this had become opportune on 9 July. The use of air presence has little to do with that. Air presence was sometimes used to show, yes, we have the means, beware, we can use them. But as I said in the phone conversation with Colonel Karremans, if you do this too frequently, so flying around without actually using air support, then in our view that would diminish its effectiveness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So the date was all important? In other words, the situation had changed so radically that Karremans' view had changed radically? Do I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Colonel Karremans thought about that is not relevant. What's relevant is what the UN leadership in Sarajevo and Zagreb thought. They are the ones who decide whether to use air support. And what mattered was that Colonel Karremans had to know the opinions at those headquarters, namely that the situation on 9 July was different from the situation on 6 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you the reason I'm asking you about Colonel Karremans is twofold. One, the Prosecution have at a very late stage decided to exhibit this particular letter, the one that I've just referred to, and secondly, the Prosecution aren't going to be call Colonel Karremans. Therefore I need to ask you about the juxtaposition of the letter and these dates. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I could understand if I saw the letter that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have it up. 2974.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So my fault, I should have put it into e-court in the first place and so you knew exactly what I was talking about, but I'm quite -- do you want to read through it again?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I'm sufficiently informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we go back to your statement, which is 6D153, please? And I've got two questions related to what I've just been asking you about, so far as dates are concerned. If we could go back to page -- if we could go to page 10 now, which is 10 in the B/C/S as well, I understand, yes, near the top of the page, that's fine, we see in the second paragraph you describing events on the 8th of July and you describe first DutchBat observation posts were surrounded and attacked, troops had to withdraw to the compound. You then briefly describe what happened to the gunner of the Dutch APC, and then in the middle of the paragraph, due to the threatening situation in the southern part of the enclave, "Colonel Karremans once again asked for air support and it was decided to carry out air presence." So if this is right, on the 8th of July, he still wanted air presence. Yet on the 9th of July, you say he was so worried about massive retaliation that he completely changed his mind. Explain that.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're going to be hearing Colonel Karremans anyway, you can ask him yourself why on 6 and 8 July he requested air support and then became fearful. I don't know why he changed his opinion about that. What I do know is why we changed our opinion at the headquarters in Sarajevo, and that was because, whereas at the beginning, only a single observation post was being threatened, and we were able to withdraw the crew from that observation post. From 8 July, a situation had materialised in which the entire enclave was under threat and using -- the air weapon was certainly being considered as a possible option.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other unrelated issue to do with dates. If we look at the first paragraph on the page in front of us, which is one sentence long, it says, "On Friday, the 7th July was rather a quiet day probably because of the bad weather conditions." I draw that to your attention because in the press release and the warning to Mladic, P2975, I don't think we need to get up at the moment, you -- it said, "the Bosnian Serb army resumed attacks against the Srebrenica enclave on Friday, 7th July, 1995." Can you explain that discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says that the attacks were taking place by 7 July, then that's not entirely correct. In any case, compared with the other days, 6 July and 8 July and 9 July, that was a relatively quiet day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on to some of the issues you've just been referring to, and that is the decision to drop bombs. Would you agree that there was a lot of indecision within UNPROFOR or perhaps I should say the UNF because of course Zagreb came into the situation?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't deny that there was some problem with taking decisions. On the one hand, this was caused by the post-air-strike guidance dated the end of May, which prescribed a highly restrictive policy about using air support. On the other hand, there was some lack of decision making in Zagreb on the evening of 10 July when despite the fact that a situation had materialised that had basically been anticipated, it took a very long time to take a decision about whether or not to provide air support, as a result of which it was not granted on 10 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, did General Janvier and Mr. Akashi have differing views from each other?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Later on, I learned from my colleagues who worked at the headquarters in Zagreb, because you understand that I wasn't present there, I learned that within the staff in Zagreb, extensive discussions took place and during these discussions, General Janvier left the meeting room several times, apparently to consult somebody else by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did your source tell you who he or she thought Janvier was speaking to?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't know. At best they could speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, of course, General Smith was absent at this time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did that add to indecision within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because there was no indecision in Sarajevo. The request for air support on 10 July was supported within a few minutes and submitted to Zagreb with a favourable recommendation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why didn't you request Smith's return to Sarajevo when he was in Geneva on the 8th of July?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not up to a Chief of Staff to request that his commander return. If General Gobillard had believed that he couldn't handle it on his own, then that was up to him. He was supposed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you discuss it with General Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That might have been regarded as a motion of distrust with respect to General Gobillard's performance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've heard one witness in this trial say that he thought that during this period, General Gobillard was spending too much time in the PTT building and not enough time with you in the Residency. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had been in General Gobillard's position, then I would have transferred my position as sector commander to my deputy and I would have been at the UNPROFOR headquarters full-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if you can't answer this, say so. Why do you think General Gobillard did not do that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I presume that he preferred being in his French surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you think the fact that not a single UN soldier in Srebrenica had been harmed by the VRS, killed or injured, influenced the indecision on the part of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber yesterday, at page 45, about the practical difficulties with the close air support when it actually happened, for example, the difficult terrain, the fact that the tanks were not all in one place, and therefore I think what you're saying is it wasn't a terribly effective tool in any event. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you think that the fact it wasn't a very effective tool was at the very least not aided by the fact that the Dutch Battalion gave up and didn't actually do any fighting themselves? In other words, there were no ground troops to support the close air support.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't believe that that affected anything. I would presume more that the fact that the arms of DutchBat was considerably inferior to the arms of the VRS were the reason to be reluctant to use weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's undoubtedly true, isn't it, that the Dutch troops negotiated with the VRS, who offered the Dutch troops to withdraw through the VRS lines without doing any harm to them, the Dutch troops? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in short, the Dutch Battalion, or certain members of that battalion, handed over their OPs to the VRS in exchange for a safe passage from the area. That's what happened, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases, they surrendered because they thought it would be too risky to withdraw across BiH lines, but during the days that followed, posts were abandoned because they were threatened by VRS troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. You're seeking to explain their action but what I put to you is correct, isn't it? Dutch troops actually handed over their OPs to the VRS in exchange for a safe passage from the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If the Court thinks the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct what? Are you answering -- are you commenting on Mr. Thayer's objection or are you answering Mr. Josse's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was answering Mr. Josse's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Anyway, he's answered and basically proves your objection wrong because in his previous answers he had not touched upon that aspect. Go ahead, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Going to move on now to the conversation that you had on the 11th of July, at about 6.00 p.m., with -- I beg your pardon, the conversation that General Gvero had on the 11th of July at about 6.00 p.m. With General Gobillard. So this is about two hours after your first conversation with Gvero. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At that point in time, had you told Gobillard of your conversation with Gvero two hours earlier?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What had you told General Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly what appears in the report of the phone conversation, that there was a particularly threatening situation to the local population in the enclave, and subsequently we discussed what else remained to be done, and after ample discussion, we decided to discontinue the air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Had Lieutenant-Colonel De Ruiter made his note of your conversation with Gvero by the point in time you talked to Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wasn't that fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so your account of the conversation was a purely oral one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Because that happened immediately after terminating the telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And presumably, it was interpreted to Gobillard by the Canadian major, Major Fortin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have a clear recollection of that, do you, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who else was present, please?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically the most important members of the UNPROFOR staff. In any case, the head of the operations section and as far as I know, also the head of the intelligence section.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have their names?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly have them in my notes but I believe that the head of the operations section was Colonel MacDonald. That was a Canadian officer. And the head of section 2 was an American officer. I believe that his name was Paopao [phoen], but if we have a break later on I can check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's why I was going to stop you. Absolutely. For my part, this is not a memory test. Quite understandably you need to look at some notes. I have absolutely no difficulty with that whatsoever. We will have a break shortly. Perhaps you can have a look at your notes. I suggest the originals. I'm not sure who's got them. And you come back and give us an answer to what I've just asked you. But I have no difficulty, and indeed at any time during the questions I ask you, I've got, I repeat, no difficulty with you referring to contemporaneous notes, that is notes that you made at the time. I contrast completely with a witness statement made sometime after the event but we don't need to get into that at the moment. Did --

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The meeting that you have just described between you, Gobillard, Fortin and these other gentlemen, was that -- was a record kept of that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As you can imagine, considering how serious the situation was, General Gobillard was present at the UNPROFOR headquarters that day, and there were constant consultations based on the situation as it developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, in fact, you've just made reference to your journal and perhaps you may have read my mind because that was my very next question. You made notes at the time, bullet-point-type notes in a diary, journal, whatever, correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the morning and evening briefings, I took notes about the most important points of the staff meeting and especially the action points that applied to me. Of course, I did not draft a report of the ongoing consultation that took place on the 11th. That would have been highly counter-productive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I may be wrong about this and this is perhaps something else you can check during the break, but I want to suggest to you that you did not mention in your journal either of your conversations with Gvero. That is the one on the 11th of July or the one on the 12th of July. You may not have any recollection of that off-hand. If you do, help us.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would have been no reason for me to record that in my book of notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Explain that, please, bearing in mind with hindsight these were rather significant conversations, to Gvero if no one else.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I primarily recorded things that I had to do in my notebook, not things that I had already done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Returning, if I may, to the conversation between Generals Gvero and Gobillard, you've described being present during some of that conversation. Do you recall how much of it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I remember being present at the start of the conversation, but that I had to leave the room fairly quickly because I had to speak on the phone elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was the setup in terms of interpreters for that conversation? Who was interpreting for General Gobillard? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Fortin acted as the interpreter for General Gobillard. And oh, you mean in the conversation with General Gvero. I think that that was the interpreter of General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you remember his or her name?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked about this previously in this interrogation. I think it was something like Zdravko but I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Zdravko?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was British.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was he in the military? Or was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was his role in relation to General Smith?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: His role was that of an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what rank did Zdravko have in the British army at that time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was he an officer? Had he been commissioned?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Don't want to be unfair about this, General Nicolai, but do you have a clear recollection of Gobillard speaking in French, Fortin translating into English, and Zdravko then speaking down the telephone in B/C/S? Is that something that sticks in your mind?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that must be how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, yes, but in your mind's eye, casting back 12 years, can you picture it actually happening, that there is -- there is a reason, believe it or not, as to why I'm asking you this in so much detail.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I can't imagine it happening any other way, but as I already told you, early on in the conversation, I was called away and that would have been why that I don't have any clear memories of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any memory of an interpreter that General Smith had called Captain Emma Bliss?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know there was a female interpreter, but I don't remember her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you have a recollection of another interpreter-cum-liaison officer called Captain Tom Dibb?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you stop? Would you stop? We are not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpretation will work now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's try again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My question was, do you have any recollection of another interpreter-cum-liaison officer called Captain Tom Dibb?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, there were several interpreters at headquarters, and I really cannot recall their names. The more so because, in most cases, I myself availed myself of the interpretation services of Svetlana.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would be a convenient moment for me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 25-minute break. How much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's going relatively slowly, I'm afraid, so I think I've got at least another hour, perhaps enough to fill the session. I won't go more than another session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see that Judge Stole is not present. You may want to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. We were just going to point out that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. That is applicable as from 9.00 this morning. Thank you, Mr. Josse. It was the first thing I had in mind of doing this morning and I was too anxious to hear your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Too kind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall, General Nicolai, the press conference that Colonel Karremans gave when he got to Zagreb soon after his departure from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And isn't it right that he said that the operation in Srebrenica had been conducted properly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, General. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have some clarification, which operation, military, the removal of the civil population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Executions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's a very, very cheap remark by my learned friend and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Come on. Let's move. Come on. General, are you in a position to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I meant in relation to the VRS military operation.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot exactly recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And he also said, didn't he, that the VRS had treated his men properly?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, returning to your evidence of yesterday, at page 54, you were asked about what impression you had gained of General Gvero after his role during this period, and you said, "I believe that he was a general who was entrusted with maintaining contact with the UN as long as General Mladic was absent because he was present in the enclave." Wasn't it Tolimir who, in fact, was your first and main point of contact at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, it was immaterial who was my contact point, as long as it was somebody with whom I could do business, and on the 8th, that was General Tolimir, and I believe also on the 9th, and the subsequent days, all of a sudden it was General Gvero but I do not know for what reason. And actually, to me, it didn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the first conversation on the 11th of July, it was you that had running the VRS wanting to speak to a general. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether I took the initiative for that call or whether I was called. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to suggest that you made the call, and in effect what you wanted was to speak to a general, any general would do, as far as you were concerned. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that I don't remember whether I myself took the initiative for this call or whether I was called. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about my proposition that as far as you were concerned, any general would do?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And were you aware that the Republika Srpska had a committee that was dedicated to dealing with the United Nations headed by Mr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if we could look at 6D7, please? This is the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska of March of 1995, and it's page -- which is headed, "Decision on forming a state committee for cooperation with United Nations and international humanitarian organisations." And it deals with -- this is being set up. We have it there in B/C/S. We now have it in English. Could we go to page 3, please? And we can see in the first paragraph that a man -- that Nikola Koljevic had been appointed the president of it, Maksim Stanisic, deputy president, and then particularly like to draw your attention in Article 2 to number 7, we see reference to a Colonel Djurdjic, coordinator for the committee's relation with the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. Were you aware of that man and his role, Colonel Djurdjic, that is?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of Professor Koljevic, I seem to remember that, but the name of Colonel Djurdjic doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So I think you probably already agreed with this: You accept that it's no more than an assumption on your part that when you spoke to Gvero that he was a person entrusted with maintaining contact with the United Nations in Mladic's absence? Do you agree with that? It's an assumption?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have P2907, please? This is your second conversation with my client, the one on the 12th of July, and in your evidence yesterday, at page 52, you were asked the following by Mr. Thayer: "Do you recall contacting the VRS Main Staff again that day in connection with issues surrounding evacuation of those refugees that you just referred to from Srebrenica?" And you said, "Yes, I remember that." -- Sorry, go on, General.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, at that point in time, after Mr. Thayer had asked what is arguably a leading question, you had not been shown the document, but in fact, that isn't what the document says, I would suggest to you. If we could go to the second page of it, second paragraph down, it says this: "General Nicolai suggested a meeting between him and BSA authorities on the matter of conditions of evacuation of DutchBat only after their support to the refugees in Srebrenica." So in fact, it was the evacuation of DutchBat that you were discussing with General Gvero, not--

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Absolutely not. The evacuation of DutchBat at that point in time was not opportune. At that point, we were only discussing the evacuation of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd rather the interruption came before the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, what's the problem, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I mean, to save a little bit of time, if we want to look at page 1, paragraph 1, I think that might clarify the issue and save some potential redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 1 deals with evacuation of the wounded specifically rather than the refugees in general, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just busy reading the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember again. I did want to talk about the evacuation of wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was the conversation ostensibly about evacuation of wounded people rather than refugees in general? That's really where we are at on this.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The negotiations about the evacuation of the entire group of refugees were conducted by Colonel Karremans with General Mladic, and Colonel Karremans would consult with me about that on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't make myself clear. Your conversation on the 12th of July at 1445 with Gvero was about the evacuation of the wounded specifically, wasn't it? It wasn't about evacuation of refugees in a general sense. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if I may digress for a moment, the evacuation of the wounded, bearing in mind everything else that had happened, was a sensible, humanitarian course of action on your part and that of the VRS, agreed?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a number of wounded people, it was necessary to receive medical treatment as soon as possible, and the quickest way of evacuating them under such circumstances is through the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you and General Gvero had a disagreement about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to press you. You haven't actually answered my question. Would you agree that the evacuation of the wounded was a sensible humanitarian course of action?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, the disagreement about the air, we see in the document. In the course of your evidence yesterday, about page 53, you explained how you were not prepared to get into a helicopter and go to Srebrenica yourself for fear that you might be shot and killed. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You should make a distinction between flights carried out with or without permission. I would have had no difficulty getting into a helicopter if the VRS authorities had said that I had permission to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you accept that the ABiH had an anti-aircraft division?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know they had anti-aircraft resources, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so what I want to suggest to you is that General Gvero's concerns about helicopters flying over the area may, in part, have been motivated by strategic considerations but was also in part concern as to what might happen to those helicopters. It was a perfectly reasonable thing to say and do, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I must tell you, there were almost daily flights over Bosnian territory, but always the authorities across whom these flights would take place would be informed of that and the flights would only take place after authority had been granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There was still a possibility, was there not, that the VRS would give permission but the helicopter be -- sorry, go on.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Had the VRS given permission and if the BiH would have had no problems, then we would have been able to evacuate the wounded by means of helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the evacuation of the refugees is concerned, you've mentioned Colonel Karremans' action in that regard. Wasn't there a high-level meeting on the 14th of July in Belgrade involving Mr. Bildt, General Smith and General Mladic to address that issue?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was such a meeting but the refugees had long been evacuated by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, asking you generally, if I may, about the two conversations that you had with General Gvero, you had never spoken to him before, as you've already told us?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You never spoke to him again?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the point of the first conversation, you had no real idea who he was other than a general in the VRS Main Staff; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You didn't know what his role was, if any, within the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that contrasts markedly with General Milovanovic whom you knew quite well as your counterpart in the VRS; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's true that he was my counterpart but as for knowing him well, I met him in person once and I also had several conversations with him via an interpreter, but that's the extent of my knowing him as a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you were able to conclude that he was General Mladic's trouble-shooter and he was a man who was able to make decisions on his own without always having to refer back to Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you had no idea, as we've just agreed, where General Gvero fitted into the scheme of things and in particular what his relationship was with Mladic, correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To state the obvious, you didn't know what was in his mind. Like any human being, you could infer from the conversation what you thought was in his mind but, of course, you didn't know what was in his mind, did you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, briefly want to ask you about an answer you gave yesterday at page 60 towards the top of that page, in relation to why you saluted at the point that Mladic was with his auxiliary personnel and he greeted the troops leaving the enclave, and as I understand it, you're saying that was to avoid embarrassment on the part of some of the members of DutchBat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then we saw on the video your having a drink with General Mladic. Was that for the same reason?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't that we were partying together. Apparently, in former Yugoslavia, it's customary to conclude certain matters with a glass of slivovitz, and certainly because I did not want to disrupt relations or certainly not -- and to ensure the undisturbed departure of DutchBat, I participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In other words, needs must, your minister had told you that you needed to get DutchBat out and if that took having a drink with Mladic, that was something you were prepared to do; is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The minister did not discuss that with me at all. The Chief of Defence Staff, the highest military staff member of the minister, explicitly instructed me that DutchBat had to leave the enclave safely. However possible and how I would take care of that, they left that to my discretion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'm right, aren't I, as far as you were concerned, the drink was, to use the English expression, needs must, and that justified your sharing the drink with Mladic in your mind?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to a different topic, if I may. You've described this one trip that you made to Srebrenica, the tail end of which I've just asked you about, but beyond that, and it may be obvious but I think it's important to spell out, you were not present in Srebrenica and therefore everything you have said about the events there are hearsay, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that I wasn't in Srebrenica at the moment the enclave was attacked?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You went there on -- I've forgotten, was it the 20th of July? I forget.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there on 21 July and I was there once before, in March 1995, when our crown prince was visiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were not there between the 1st and the 20th of July, when the enclave fell and the events that surround this case occurred, were you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And therefore, everything you have told us about those events, as to what actually occurred in and around the enclave, is hearsay, stands to reason, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would seem to be clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You, in common with everyone, received confused and diverse reports as to what was going on in that enclave over that two-week period?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I received the standard reports from DutchBat but DutchBat had very limited information at that point as well because they were no longer able to leave their compound, and otherwise there were all kinds of rumours but many were never confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So there were rumours, you received information from the BiH side with whom UNPROFOR shared fairly cordial relations, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no difference between our relationship with the BiH and that with the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My question, with its pejorative remark, deserved that answer, and I apologise. That wasn't what I was driving at. Would you agree that you received information from the Muslim side as to what was going on in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that at that time the BiH didn't have information about exactly what was happening in the enclave either because they didn't have any people there at that moment. Their people had all left the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me try and cut this short. Perhaps you won't agree with this, but information was scant and confused in the two weeks that I'm asking about. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is beyond dispute, isn't it, that Srebrenica had not been demilitarised as of July 1995. In other words, before the VRS attack on the enclave. It had not been demilitarised, had it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me qualify that. It was not demilitarised to the extent that we would have liked it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There were attacks, were there not, from within the enclave to the outside on occasion? Go on.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And some of these attacks resulted in Serb civilians being killed, correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were unable to verify that information because the Serbs did not allow us, did not give us freedom of movement across Serbian territory and then it's difficult to verify that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware, for example, of an attack on a village called Visnjica on the 26th of June of 1995, where the village was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this specific case, but the VRS did complain repeatedly about attacks on Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you agree that UNPROFOR was not prepared to do anything about this?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I definitely do not agree with you about that. We were certainly willing to do something about that. But if the parties involved don't give you freedom of movement and in addition they block the fuel that you need to do this, then of course your means are extremely limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you're saying because the fuel wasn't getting into the enclave, your Dutch Battalion were unable to carry out their tasks, which would otherwise have meant they would have properly demilitarised the enclave? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not exactly what you're hearing me say. What you're hearing me say is that due to lack of fuel and lack of freedom of movement or limited freedom of movement, we were able to carry out only part of our duties and certainly not to the extent we would have liked to. Whether we could have fully demilitarised the enclave if we had had fuel, you didn't hear me say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Serbs complained to UNPROFOR about the fact that it was not demilitarised, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did that several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And significantly, UNPROFOR knew that the Serbs were likely to do something about it in due course.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can never say anything for sure, but, of course, that was a possibility. I did tell the VRS repeatedly that the -- they were in part responsible for the fact that we were not in a position to do our duties properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You knew that apart from the fact that the Serbs were asserting that there were raids taking place from the enclave to the outside and civilians were being killed, they also -- you, UNPROFOR, also knew that the eastern enclaves and the fact that they were not demilitarised was a serious drain on the VRS manpower and that manpower was required in a different part of Bosnia; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The intrinsic existence of the enclave is already very troop-intensive for a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we know that it came as no surprise to General Smith, and presumably no surprise to you, when the VRS started an attack on the enclave.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did expect something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, indeed, I want to look with you at a document that we began to examine yesterday, which is 6D204. And this, you'll remember, is from General Janvier to Mr. Annan among others dated the 10th of July, and it's the daily sit-rep and it includes, as I mentioned yesterday, quite a detailed military assessment of the situation in Srebrenica. And if we go to page 5, I'd like to look at this in a little bit of detail with you, if I may. Perhaps before -- sorry, perhaps before that's done, it might help if we went back to the first page, simply for completeness and I asked you was this document sent to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We see a list of groups it was sent to as information. I'm afraid it's real UN-speak to me and I can't assist. Can you, as to whether it went to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR does not appear here, but I admit that I don't know who is included under the word "list" which appears twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. To page 5, please. We have this military assessment here, and it begins by saying, "By attacking the Srebrenica enclave, the BSA probably wants to achieve the following aims." And then I'm not going to read out the next five points but perhaps we could all read it to ourselves.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then mentions the -- something to do with Gorazde, which is -- well, by all means, read it. It might be an idea if you read the next paragraph and read on, because otherwise, I might be accused of taking this out of context. In that long paragraph it says, "However, at present there are no indications suggesting this." And then when you've got to the bottom of the page, General, I'll invite us to go to the next page. Then there is a paragraph where the prediction says, "the BSA is not expected to seize the safe area."

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then it says, I'm going to read it out: "The Bosnian Serbs could halt their advance pending a number of conditions, the complete demilitarisation of the enclave will probably be their highest priority. This would also serve their primary goal of freeing troops from around the enclave." So as far as the author of this report was concerned, and seems to be General Janvier, at least it's gone out in his name, that's what he perceived at that time as being what was in the minds of the VRS. Do you read it like that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the assessment by General Janvier's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
